blocks.content: Open WhatsApp and a message lands the instant it is sent. Watch a cab on the Uber map and it glides along the road on its own. Open a Google Doc and you see other people typing live. A stock ticker keeps ticking with no refresh.
In every case the server reaches out to the client the moment something changes. Nobody pressed refresh. That is real time communication.

It goes against how the web normally works. The web is built on request and response: the client asks, the server answers, done. Real time needs the opposite, the server has to deliver news the instant it happens.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785278116181-221860250.png
blocks.alt: The server pushes to the client the moment something changes

blocks.content: 1. What Real Time Communication Means
Real time communication means data reaches the user almost instantly after an event, without the user asking for it.
For a human, almost instantly means within roughly 100 to 300 milliseconds. Faster than that and it feels alive, slower and it feels laggy.
You see it everywhere once you look:

["Chat, where a message appears the moment it is sent","Live feeds, like sports scores, stock prices, and dashboards","Presence, like the green dot showing who is online and who is typing","Collaboration, where many people edit one document and see each other cursors","Location, like a delivery rider moving on a live map"]
items: Chat, where a message appears the moment it is sent
Live feeds, like sports scores, stock prices, and dashboards
Presence, like the green dot showing who is online and who is typing
Collaboration, where many people edit one document and see each other cursors
Location, like a delivery rider moving on a live map

blocks.title: The real challenge
blocks.content: The hard part is not showing the update. It is getting the server to reach the client the instant something happens, on a web that was designed for the client to ask first.
So the real question is how the server reaches the client at all. That comes down to two models.
There are only two ways for a client to get data from a server, and the whole topic hinges on this difference.
["Pull: the client keeps asking, is there anything new. The server almost always answers, no.","Push: the server sends data to the client the moment it changes, with no request needed."]
items: Pull: the client keeps asking, is there anything new. The server almost always answers, no.
Push: the server sends data to the client the moment it changes, with no request needed.

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785278118499-226565936.png
blocks.alt: Pull keeps asking and mostly gets nothing; push sends only on change

blocks.content: Normal web requests are pull based. Pull is a poor fit for real time, because the client either asks too often and wastes work, or too rarely and shows stale data. Every real time technique is really a clever way to get push behavior on top of the web.
2. Short Polling
Short polling is the crudest form of pull. The client asks the server on a fixed timer, say every three seconds, whether anything is new.
Watch the timing and the waste becomes obvious.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785278120162-347522182.png
blocks.alt: Short polling: fixed timer requests, mostly empty, updates arrive late

blocks.content: Two problems jump out. Updates can be late by up to the polling interval, and the vast majority of requests return nothing at all.

The cost is real at scale. Imagine one million users polling every three seconds. That is more than three hundred thousand requests every second, and almost all of them return an empty response. You are paying for a flood of requests that carry no news.

blocks.title: When short polling is still fine
blocks.content: If updates are rare and a delay of a few seconds is acceptable, short polling is genuinely the simplest thing that works. Do not over engineer a status page.
3. Long Polling

Long polling keeps the simplicity of HTTP but removes most of the waste. The client sends a request, and instead of replying immediately with nothing, the server holds the request open until it actually has data, then responds.
The client gets the update with almost no delay, then instantly opens another request. It feels close to real time while using only ordinary HTTP.
This technique has its own dedicated page in this section, which walks through the request lifecycle, the cursor trick, and how to scale it.
4. Server Sent Events
Server sent events, or SSE, flip the model. The client opens one connection, and then the server streams events down it for as long as it stays open. It is one directional, server to client only.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785278121765-92119629.png
blocks.alt: SSE: one connection open, then the server streams many events down it

blocks.content: The browser supports it natively through the EventSource API, and it reconnects automatically if the connection drops, even resuming from the last event id.
SSE shines for feeds that flow one way: a stock ticker, live match commentary, a notifications bell, a build or deployment log streaming to your screen.

["One way, server to client","Runs over plain HTTP, so proxies and load balancers handle it easily","Automatic reconnection with a last event id","Not the right tool when the client also needs to send messages often"]
items: One way, server to client
Runs over plain HTTP, so proxies and load balancers handle it easily
Automatic reconnection with a last event id
Not the right tool when the client also needs to send messages often

blocks.content: 5. WebSockets
WebSockets open a single, persistent, two way channel between client and server. Once it is open, either side can send a message at any instant, with almost no overhead per message.
It begins life as a normal HTTP request that asks to upgrade, and after the server agrees the same connection is kept open and switched to the WebSocket protocol.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785278123311-250868447.png
blocks.alt: WebSocket: an HTTP upgrade, then a persistent two way connection

blocks.content: This is what powers the apps that feel truly live. WhatsApp and Slack messaging, multiplayer games, and collaborative editors like Figma and Google Docs all lean on WebSockets, because both sides are constantly sending.

blocks.title: The cost of a persistent connection
blocks.content: Every open WebSocket holds memory on the server for as long as the user is connected, and you must handle reconnection and scaling yourself. Reach for it only when the interaction is genuinely two way and frequent.
6. WebRTC
WebRTC is the odd one out. Instead of every message passing through your server, it sets up a direct connection between two clients, which is exactly what you want for audio and video.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785278125025-557513457.png
blocks.alt: WebRTC: a signaling server helps peers meet, then media flows directly

blocks.content: A server is still needed at the very start, to help the two peers discover each other and exchange connection details. This step is called signaling. After that, the audio and video flow directly between the two devices for the lowest possible latency.
Use WebRTC for video calls, voice, and screen sharing, the way Zoom and Google Meet do. For almost everything else, SSE or WebSockets are simpler to build and operate.
7. Comparing and Choosing a Technique
Laid side by side, the tradeoffs become clear. Notice how the direction of data is usually what decides the choice.

{"headers":["Technique","Direction","Connection","Best for","Real examples"],"rows":[["Short polling","Client asks repeatedly","New request each time","Simple, infrequent updates","Basic status checks"],["Long polling","Client asks, server holds","Reopened after each response","Near real time on plain HTTP","Older Gmail and Facebook chat"],["SSE","Server to client only","One long lived connection","Live feeds and notifications","Stock tickers, live scores"],["WebSockets","Two way","One persistent connection","Chat, games, collaboration","WhatsApp, Slack, Figma"],["WebRTC","Peer to peer","Direct between clients","Audio and video","Zoom, Google Meet"]]}
The progression is historical too. Short polling came first, long polling made it less wasteful, SSE added true server push, and WebSockets added full two way communication.
Knowing the options is one thing, picking the right one for a given problem is the real skill.
The fastest way to pick is to ask who needs to talk and how often. Three concrete examples:
A stock price dashboard: data only flows from the server to the browser, many times a second. This is a textbook fit for SSE, one connection streaming prices down.
A team chat app: both sides send constantly, messages, typing indicators, read receipts. That two way, high frequency traffic is why chat uses WebSockets.
A video call: the media is huge and must be as low latency as possible, and it does not belong on your servers. WebRTC connects the two people directly.
A simple rule: if the client mostly listens, use SSE. If client and server talk back and forth constantly, use WebSockets. If two users exchange audio or video, use WebRTC.
8. Delivery, Ordering, and Live Features
Real time is not only about speed, it is also about correctness. Once the server is pushing messages, you must decide what happens to ordering, loss, and duplicates.

["Ordering: messages should usually arrive in the order they were sent. A single WebSocket preserves order, but a fan out broker can reorder them unless you are careful.","At least once: a message may arrive more than once, so clients should be ready to ignore duplicates.","At most once: a message may be lost, which is fine for a live price but not for a chat message.","Exactly once: the hardest to guarantee and rarely worth the cost."]
items: Ordering: messages should usually arrive in the order they were sent. A single WebSocket preserves order, but a fan out broker can reorder them unless you are careful.
At least once: a message may arrive more than once, so clients should be ready to ignore duplicates.
At most once: a message may be lost, which is fine for a live price but not for a chat message.
Exactly once: the hardest to guarantee and rarely worth the cost.

blocks.content: For chat you usually want ordered, at least once delivery with a message id so the client can drop duplicates. For a price feed, a lost tick does not matter because a newer one is right behind it.

blocks.title: A practical trick
blocks.content: Attach a monotonic id or sequence number to every message. It lets the client detect gaps, reorder if needed, and drop duplicates, which quietly solves most delivery problems.
These same guarantees quietly power the small live features users notice most.
The small live touches in modern apps are all real time features built on the same techniques.

["Presence: the green dot showing who is online, kept fresh with periodic heartbeats over the connection.","Typing indicators: a short lived signal one client sends that the server relays to others in the room.","Read receipts: an event sent back when a message is seen, updating the sender in real time."]
items: Presence: the green dot showing who is online, kept fresh with periodic heartbeats over the connection.
Typing indicators: a short lived signal one client sends that the server relays to others in the room.
Read receipts: an event sent back when a message is seen, updating the sender in real time.

blocks.content: These features feel magical but are cheap. They are tiny messages over a connection that is already open, which is another reason a persistent WebSocket is convenient once you have one.
9. Scaling Real Time Systems

Real time systems are stateful, and that is what makes them hard. Every connected user is holding an open connection on one specific server, unlike a normal stateless request that any server can handle.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785278126708-835374964.png
blocks.alt: Scaling: a broker fans events to every server, which push to its own clients

blocks.content: Two problems follow from that. First, a user is pinned to one server, so a normal round robin load balancer will break them, and you need sticky sessions or a connection aware balancer. Second, when an event happens on one server, every other server also has connected users who need it.

["Pin connections with sticky sessions or a connection aware load balancer","Fan out through a broker, so an event is published to Redis or Kafka and delivered to every server, which then pushes to its own clients","Respect memory limits, since each open connection costs memory, which is the classic C10K and now C10M challenge of holding huge numbers of connections on one machine"]
items: Pin connections with sticky sessions or a connection aware load balancer
Fan out through a broker, so an event is published to Redis or Kafka and delivered to every server, which then pushes to its own clients
Respect memory limits, since each open connection costs memory, which is the classic C10K and now C10M challenge of holding huge numbers of connections on one machine

blocks.content: 10. Fallbacks and Security
Not every network allows WebSockets. Strict corporate proxies, old firewalls, and some mobile networks block them, so a robust system degrades instead of breaking.
The common strategy is a fallback chain: try WebSockets first, fall back to SSE, and fall back again to long polling if needed. Libraries like Socket.IO do this automatically behind one simple API.

["Try WebSockets for full two way, low latency communication","Fall back to SSE when the client only needs to receive","Fall back to long polling when even SSE is blocked","Always keep reconnect and resume logic underneath every option"]
items: Try WebSockets for full two way, low latency communication
Fall back to SSE when the client only needs to receive
Fall back to long polling when even SSE is blocked
Always keep reconnect and resume logic underneath every option

blocks.content: Once connections are reliable, the next concern is keeping them secure.
A long lived connection still needs authentication and authorization, and it is easy to get wrong because the usual per request checks do not apply the same way.

["Use wss, the encrypted form of WebSockets, just as you use https","Authenticate at connection time, usually by passing a token during the handshake","Check the Origin header to prevent cross site connection hijacking","Re verify authorization for sensitive actions, since a connection can stay open long after a token expires","Rate limit messages per connection so a single client cannot flood the server"]
items: Use wss, the encrypted form of WebSockets, just as you use https
Authenticate at connection time, usually by passing a token during the handshake
Check the Origin header to prevent cross site connection hijacking
Re verify authorization for sensitive actions, since a connection can stay open long after a token expires
Rate limit messages per connection so a single client cannot flood the server

blocks.content: 11. The Evolution From Polling to Push
blocks.text: 11. The Evolution From Polling to Push

blocks.content: It helps to see these techniques as a story, each one fixing the flaw of the last.

["Short polling: ask on a timer, simple but wasteful and laggy","Long polling: hold the request open, near real time on plain HTTP","SSE: a true one way server push over a single connection","WebSockets: a full two way persistent channel","WebRTC: a direct peer to peer channel for audio and video"]
items: Short polling: ask on a timer, simple but wasteful and laggy
Long polling: hold the request open, near real time on plain HTTP
SSE: a true one way server push over a single connection
WebSockets: a full two way persistent channel
WebRTC: a direct peer to peer channel for audio and video

blocks.content: Knowing this progression is useful in an interview, because it lets you justify a choice by explaining exactly what problem each step solved.
12. Common Mistakes

["Using short polling at scale, which floods the server with empty requests","Reaching for WebSockets when data only flows one way, where SSE would be simpler","Forgetting that connections are stateful and trying to load balance them like normal requests","Skipping reconnection logic, so a dropped connection silently stops updates","Ignoring backpressure, where the server pushes faster than a slow client can consume"]
items: Using short polling at scale, which floods the server with empty requests
Reaching for WebSockets when data only flows one way, where SSE would be simpler
Forgetting that connections are stateful and trying to load balance them like normal requests
Skipping reconnection logic, so a dropped connection silently stops updates
Ignoring backpressure, where the server pushes faster than a slow client can consume

blocks.content: 13. HLD Interview: How to Talk About This
blocks.text: 13. HLD Interview: How to Talk About This

blocks.content: When a design needs live updates, name the technique and defend it in one breath.
Lead with direction: I first ask whether data flows one way or both ways. One way from the server points to SSE, two way points to WebSockets.
Reject short polling out loud: I mention that short polling wastes huge numbers of requests at scale, and that long polling or SSE is the better baseline.
Plan the stateful part: Real time connections live on a specific server, so I add sticky sessions and a pub sub broker like Redis to fan events across servers.
Name the tradeoff: WebSockets give the lowest latency and full two way messaging, but they cost memory per connection and need care to scale, so I use them only when the interaction truly needs it.
